title: Corsankell: James and his sons
standfirst: A teind list and a 1571 charter give a rare stated father-and-sons group at Corsankell. The household is real; its place in the wider Glasgow story is not yet demonstrated.
question: How did the Corsankell household connect to William's Glasgow burgh family?
answer: The 1571 NRS catalogue abstract names James elder's sons James and John, while the 1559–60 teind list places elder and younger James at Corsankell. It does not identify James elder's father, establish the city connection, or securely identify the named John with a later Kilwinning profile.

chapters.title: Two Jameses at Corsankell
body: The teind material distinguishes James elder from James younger at the Stevenston holding.
The labels establish a local household setting but do not on their own say how the men were related.

chapters.title: The charter supplies the relationship
body: The 1571 charter explicitly calls James and John sons of James elder.
The record-defined John is represented by Glasgow-4061; a different Kilwinning John remains only a possible match.

clusters.title: James elder, James and John
clusters.summary: The charter identifies two sons of James elder at the Corsankell holding.
clusters.boundary: It does not provide a burgh ancestor, a wife, or the later identity of John.

proved: James and John were sons of James elder
hypothesis: a connection to the Glasgow burgh family
unresolved: the Kilwinning identity of the younger John

gaps.title: Inspect the original 1571 deed
gaps.why: It may preserve a predecessor, relative or holding history beyond the catalogue abstract.

gaps.title: Trace earlier estate succession
gaps.why: A documented transfer could test the proposed burgh bridge.
